assignments.description:
A01 — Unofficial transcript

Due: Wednesday of Semester Kick Off Week, by end of day.

Your unofficial transcript is the "receipt" of your college journey so far:

  • Transcript = what you've done
  • Progress report (A02) = what you still need
  • Degree plan (A03) = how you're going to finish strong

What students will submit

Submit two files in Canvas:

  1. Transcript PDF — export/download your unofficial transcript as a PDF. File name: {COURSE}_A01_UnofficialTranscript_Last_First_Year_Semester.pdf
  2. Quick reflection (short write-up) — a short reflection as PDF or Markdown. File name: {COURSE}_A01_TranscriptReflection_Last_First_Year_Semester.pdf (or .md)

Requirements

Part 1 — Get your unofficial transcript (PDF)

  • Log in to your institution's student portal / single sign-on.
  • Open the self-service system.
  • Find "Unofficial Transcript."
  • Download/export as PDF.
  • Confirm the PDF opens and looks readable (not blank, not sideways, not one pixel tall).
  • Look at your GPA and make sure you can live with it, or have a plan to fix it.
  • Check for any transfer credit that should be there but is missing.
  • Give it a vibe check for anything that feels off from your lived experience.

Part 2 — Reflection (answer all prompts)

In 5–10 sentences total, answer:

  • What surprised you when you looked at your transcript?
  • What's one thing you're proud of so far?
  • What's one thing you want to improve this semester (study habits, attendance, time management, asking for help, etc.)?
  • Any issues to flag (missing credit, repeated course, transfer credit weirdness, hold, incorrect grade posting)?

If you spot something that looks wrong, that's not "bad news" — that's useful intel. Bring it up early so it can get fixed.

Privacy / safety rules (important)

  • Do not post your transcript anywhere public (GitHub, Discord, etc.).
  • Submit only through Canvas.
  • If your transcript contains sensitive information (it often does), keep it private and don't share it with classmates.

Common problems + fixes

  • "I can't find the transcript option." Search your self-service system for "transcript" and look for "unofficial transcript."
  • "My transcript looks wrong." Submit what you can and mention the issue in your reflection — it'll get handled together.
  • "I have a hold and can't access it." Submit a screenshot of the hold message (if allowed) and write what happened in the reflection.

Notes (instructor)

This pairs with A02 (Progress Report) and A03 (Degree Plan). Goal: know what it takes to graduate — identify issues early, and start planning with accurate data. See rubrics/A01_rubric.md for grading.
assignments.name: A01 — Unofficial transcript

rubric.long_description: Submitted, readable, correct document
Answers all prompts with real effort (not one-word responses)
File naming + submission is clean and on time

assignments.description:
A02 — Progress report

Due: Wednesday of Semester Kick Off Week, by end of day.

Why we're doing this

Your progress report (from the registrar) is the closest thing to "the truth in writing" about your degree requirements. It shows what you've completed, what still remains, and where your gaps are. This assignment makes sure you know how to find it and how to read it — the same software that runs your graduation check produces this report.

What you will submit

Submit two items:

  1. Progress Report PDF — export your progress report from your institution's self-service system as a PDF.
  2. Short summary — either a Canvas text entry, or a second page in the same PDF.

File naming (PDF): {COURSE}_A02_ProgressReport_Last_First_Year_Semester.pdf — e.g. CS1_A02_ProgressReport_Evert_Jeremy_2003_Fall.pdf.

Step-by-step instructions (how to get the report)

  1. Log in to your institution's single sign-on.
  2. Open self-service (the same system where you access other student tools).
  3. Search for "Progress Report."
  4. Open your report and export/download as PDF.
  5. Save it somewhere you can find it again — you'll use it again for A01.

Summary requirements (your written part)

Write 6–10 sentences that answer these prompts:

  1. What degree/major does the progress report show?
  2. What areas/categories are listed (Gen Ed, major core, electives, etc.)?
  3. List 3 specific requirements you still need (courses or requirement blocks).
  4. Identify one thing that surprised you, or one part you don't understand yet.
  5. What's your next step? (E.g. "I need to ask an advisor about ," or "I need to plan when I'll take .")

If something looks wrong

If anything seems incorrect or missing, say so in your summary and include the exact section name you're referencing. Don't panic — just document it.

Need help?

If you can't find the report or something looks unexpected, message the instructor.

See rubrics/A02_rubric.md for grading.
assignments.name: A02 — Progress report

rubric.long_description: Successfully submitted
Meets requirements (all 5 prompts answered, complete, clear)
Real requirement names / real sections referenced, not vague

assignments.description:
A03 — Personal semester-by-semester degree plan

Due: Wednesday of Semester Kick Off Week, by end of day.

Why we're doing this

This assignment helps you build a realistic plan for graduation. You'll use your unofficial transcript (A01), progress report (A02), and your institution's catalog/schedule to map out your remaining semesters and confirm prerequisites and course availability. Connect the dots and land on the semester you actually expect to graduate.

This is a planning tool you should keep and update all semester — bring it to advising appointments. (Tape it to your wall for the days you want to give up.)

What you will submit

Upload one PDF, exported from a spreadsheet (Excel or Google Sheets).

File naming: {COURSE}_A03_DegreePlan_Last_First_Year_Semester.pdf — e.g. CS1_A03_DegreePlan_Evert_Jeremy_2003_Fall.pdf.

Requirements (what must be in your spreadsheet)

1) Title + basics (top of page) — your name; major (and minor if applicable); option (if applicable); your expected graduation semester (e.g. "Spring 2028").

2) Semester-by-semester plan (the main table) — list every semester from now until graduation. For each planned course: course prefix/number, course name, credits, and optional notes ("needs prereq," "only offered fall," etc.). For each semester: total credits.

3) Prerequisites + reality check — show evidence you checked your institution's course catalog/schedule offerings, your progress report (what remains), and your unofficial transcript (what's completed). This can be a short "checked list," notes in a dedicated column, or a small "Verification" box.

4) Two scenarios (minimum) — e.g. Scenario A (~12 credits/semester) and Scenario B (~18 credits/semester with summer classes). For each, show the expected graduation term and what changes between the two plans.

5) Advising notes / questions — a short list (minimum 2 items) of questions or notes for an advisor, e.g. "Is Course X offered every spring?" or "Do I need an elective in category Y?"

Step-by-step instructions (how to build it)

  1. Open Excel or Google Sheets.
  2. Create a sheet named "Degree Plan."
  3. Add your title + graduation target at the top.
  4. Build your main table (suggested columns: Semester | Course # | Course Name | Credits | Notes).
  5. Add semester totals (a SUM at the bottom of each semester block works).
  6. Duplicate the sheet (or add a second section) for Scenario B.
  7. Export as PDF (Excel: File → Export → Create PDF; Google Sheets: File → Download → PDF).

Late / revision notes

If something doesn't make sense (missing prereqs, unsure offering), mark it clearly as a question — don't guess silently. Planning is allowed to be imperfect; hiding uncertainty is not.

Need help?

If anything looks unexpected in your progress report or transcript, message the instructor.

See rubrics/A03_rubric.md for grading.
assignments.name: A03 — Personal semester-by-semester degree plan

rubric.long_description: All semesters + courses listed through to graduation
Credits, prerequisites considered, offerings checked
Included and clearly explained (e.g. 12 cr/semester vs. 18 cr/semester + summer)
Readable, labeled, totals included
Correct format + filename

assignments.description:
A08 — Degree Reflection

Due: Wednesday of Semester Kick Off Week, alongside A01–A03, by end of day.

Why this is a separate assignment

A01–A03 prove you can find the data (transcript, progress report, degree plan) and read it correctly. This assignment is graded on whether you actually thought about what that data means for you. It is deliberately not a paragraph folded into the end of A01 or A03 — it is its own assignment, with its own points, and every question below is its own graded line. Reflection is the part of Semester Kick Off Week that's easiest to skip when it's buried as an afterthought in another assignment's write-up. Making it separate, numbered, and individually pointed is this course's way of saying: this isn't filler, it's the point of the week.

Where this structure comes from

The questions below borrow their shape from two goal-setting/productivity frameworks — Michael Hyatt's Your Best Year Ever (naming what excites you and what you're afraid of, then converting both into a real plan) and Free to Focus (sorting what's ahead of you instead of just reacting to it). You don't need to have read either book. The questions stand on their own; the framework just explains why they're shaped the way they are, in case you're curious.

Using an LLM here (encouraged, with one boundary)

Use an LLM to think wider, not to think for you:

  • Stuck on Q5 (three mitigating ideas)? Ask an LLM to brainstorm eight or ten, then pick your own three and say why.
  • Not sure what a class or requirement actually involves? Ask an LLM to summarize a syllabus or department page you paste in, then react to that summary in your own words.

The choice, the reasoning, and the plan have to be yours. An LLM that writes your answer for you defeats the purpose — this assignment exists to find out what you think about your own degree, not what a model guesses a good student would say. Grading can tell the difference (see rubrics/A08_rubric.md): a generic, could-be-anyone answer scores lower than a specific one, regardless of how polished the writing is.

What you will submit

A Canvas text entry (no file upload) with nine numbered answers, answered individually — don't merge them into one essay. Numbering them separately is what makes each one gradable, and visible, on its own.

Part 1 — What excites you

Q1. Which class or requirement still ahead of you excites you the most? Name it specifically — a course number and title if it's a single course, or the exact requirement category (e.g. "the lab science requirement," not "gen eds" or "a science class") if it isn't tied to one course yet — and say why. (2 pts)

Q2. What's the best use of your time between now and when you take it, so you actually get the most out of it — not just survive it? (2 pts)

Q3. How does that class connect to the career you're aiming for? Name the specific job-market skill or requirement it builds toward — be concrete, not "it'll help in general." (2 pts)

Part 2 — What worries you

Q4. What are you afraid of for your degree — a specific class, requirement, or milestone? Name it. ("Math" is not an answer; "Calculus II, because I barely passed Calculus I" is.) (2 pts)

Q5. List three mitigating ideas for that situation — three genuinely different approaches, not three phrasings of the same one idea. (3 pts — 1 per distinct, real idea)

Q6. Which of the three is your favorite — the one you'll actually act on? Why that one, and not the other two? (2 pts)

Q7. Given that choice, what's the best use of your time between now and when you face it? (2 pts)

Q8. How will closing this gap help your career — what specific job-market skill or requirement does it protect? (2 pts)

Part 3 — Why it matters

Q9. Look back at your A03 degree plan. Name one place it truly reflects what you value, and one place it doesn't yet — and what would have to change (in the plan, or in you) to close that gap. (3 pts)

Total: 20 points

Need help?

If a question doesn't apply cleanly to your situation (undeclared major, transferring soon, etc.), answer it for the closest real version of your situation and say so — don't skip it silently.

See rubrics/A08_rubric.md for grading.
assignments.name: A08 — Degree Reflection

rubric.long_description: Q1 (2 pts) — names a specific exciting course/requirement with a real personal reason, not a generic "I like this subject." Q2 (2 pts) — a concrete action before that class, not "study hard." Q3 (2 pts) — a specific job-market skill/requirement it connects to, not "it'll help in general."

Q4 (2 pts) — names a specific feared class/requirement/milestone, not a vague subject area. Q5 (3 pts total, 1 pt per genuinely distinct mitigating idea, up to 3 — three restatements of one idea score 1, not 3) — three mitigating ideas. Q6 (2 pts) — a real reason for the favorite idea: fit, feasibility, or past experience, not "I don't know, this one."
Q7 (2 pts) — a concrete action tied to the specific idea chosen in Q6. Q8 (2 pts) — names a specific job-market skill/requirement that closing the gap protects.
Names one specific point of fit and one specific point of tension with A03, plus what would change to close it (one holistic 0–3 judgment, not sub-divided further).

assignments.description:
A04 — Resume

Due: Friday of Semester Kick Off Week, by 4:00 PM.

Why we're doing this

Your resume is a living document, not a one-time chore before you need a job. This assignment kicks off the habit: get a real, current resume on file now, then keep building it all semester with the 3-2-1 CV/resume habit taught earlier today (3 daily notes, 2 weekly CV paragraphs, 1 monthly resume bullet).

This is a first draft. There's a check-in later in the semester where you revisit and strengthen it — this version just needs to be real and current, not perfect.

Remember: CV = your full story. Resume = your best highlights for one job. If you kept the 3-2-1 habit going since Week 1, this is curation, not a panic-write.

What you will submit

Upload one document (PDF preferred; Word is acceptable).

File naming: {COURSE}_A04_Resume_Last_First_Year_Semester.pdf — e.g. CS1_A04_Resume_Evert_Jeremy_2003_Fall.pdf.

Requirements

1) Create or update your resume. Include sections for contact information, work experience, education, skills, and accomplishments.

  • Recent high school graduate? Include relevant high school achievements (leadership, activities, awards, work).
  • Been out of school a while? Focus on your more recent accomplishments.

2) Use achievement framing, not duty framing. Apply the STAR bullet formula from Friday of Semester Kick Off Week: [Power verb] + [what you did / context] + [result or benefit]. "Resolved 15+ customer issues per shift, improving satisfaction" beats "Responsible for customer service."

3) Save it as a document you'll keep updating. This isn't a one-time submission — you'll be adding to it and refining it throughout the semester.

Getting feedback

  • Visit Career Services or the Writing Center.
  • Ask your advisor, an instructor, or a mentor to review it.
  • Watch a LinkedIn Learning video on resume writing for extra tips.

Need help?

If you don't have much work experience yet, ask the instructor — projects, coursework, and volunteer work all count.

See rubrics/A04_rubric.md for grading.
assignments.name: A04 — Resume

rubric.long_description: Contact info, work experience, education, skills, accomplishments all present
Bullets use STAR/power-verb framing (achievements, not just duties)
File naming + submission is clean and on time

assignments.description:
A05 — Dream Job Paper

Due: Friday of Semester Kick Off Week, by 4:00 PM.

Why we're doing this

This isn't a hypothetical exercise. Naming a real job you could actually apply for — now or in a few years — turns "career" from a vague worry into a specific target you can plan toward. It also feeds directly into A06 — Professional Gap Analysis, due the following week: you can't measure the gap between where you are and where you're going until you've named where you're going.

What you will submit

A short paper (roughly 1–2 pages, or as your instructor specifies).

File naming: {COURSE}_A05_DreamJobPaper_Last_First_Year_Semester.pdf — e.g. CS1_A05_DreamJobPaper_Evert_Jeremy_2003_Fall.pdf.

Requirements

1) Choose a specific, real dream job. Not "something in tech" or "something creative" — an actual job title/role you could realistically apply for, whether now or after you finish your degree.

2) Research the job. Look into:

  • Education, skills, and experience it requires
  • Day-to-day responsibilities and typical work environment
  • Career advancement opportunities from that role

3) Write an essay covering:

  • Why this is your dream job — what excites you about it, what you find most appealing.
  • How it aligns with your skills and interests — how your current skills, education, and experience make you a fit (or what's missing — that's fair game to name here, you'll dig into it in A06).
  • What it would take to get there — a realistic first step or two.

Need help?

If you're not sure what you want yet, that's normal — pick the closest real target you can find and treat this as a first draft of a direction, not a lifetime contract.

See rubrics/A05_rubric.md for grading.
assignments.name: A05 — Dream Job Paper

rubric.long_description: A concrete, realistically-applicable job title/role, not a vague field
Requirements, responsibilities, environment, and advancement covered
Explains why it's the dream job and how it aligns with current skills/interests

assignments.description:
A06 — Professional Gap Analysis

Due: Friday of Semester Kick Off Week, by 4:00 PM.

Why we're doing this

Knowing your dream job (A05) is only half the picture. This assignment compares who you are right now against what that job actually requires — so your remaining semesters (and your degree plan from Semester Kick Off Week's A03) can target real gaps instead of guessing.

What you will submit

A short written analysis (roughly 1–2 pages, or as your instructor specifies).

File naming: {COURSE}_A06_GapAnalysis_Last_First_Year_Semester.pdf — e.g. CS1_A06_GapAnalysis_Evert_Jeremy_2003_Fall.pdf.

Requirements

1) Name your target job. Use the dream job from A05 (or refine it if your thinking has changed since then).

2) Assess your current skillset. List what you currently have — both hard skills (technical abilities) and soft skills (communication, teamwork, leadership, etc.).

3) Conduct the gap analysis. Compare your current skillset against what the job actually requires. Name the specific skills and qualifications you're missing.

4) Build an action plan. For each gap, name a concrete action (a course, a certification, a project, an internship, relevant experience) and a realistic timeline for closing it.

5) Reflect. A few sentences on what you learned from doing this analysis — anything that surprised you, or changed how you're thinking about your remaining semesters.

Need help?

If you're not sure what a job actually requires, look at real job postings for that role, not just a job title's general reputation.

See rubrics/A06_rubric.md for grading.
assignments.name: A06 — Professional Gap Analysis

rubric.long_description: Real hard + soft skills listed, not generic filler
Specific, named gaps between current skillset and target job requirements
Concrete actions (courses, certifications, projects, experience) with realistic timelines
Genuine sentence-level reflection on what the analysis revealed

assignments.description:
A09 — Career Reflection

Due: Friday of Semester Kick Off Week, alongside A04–A06, by 4:00 PM.

Why this is a separate assignment

A04–A06 prove you can build a resume, name a real target job, and compare your skills against it. This assignment is graded on whether you actually thought about what that target job means for you — what you're looking forward to, and what genuinely worries you about it. Like A08, it's separate from A04–A06 on purpose, with its own points on its own numbered lines, so there's no ambiguity about whether reflection is optional. It isn't.

Where this structure comes from

Part 1 borrows from the idea of a "Desire Zone" (from Michael Hyatt's Free to Focus) — the parts of a job where you're both good at the work and genuinely want to do it, as opposed to work you can do but dread. Part 2 borrows from the same book's sorting habit — name the hard thing honestly, then find a real way to handle it, rather than hoping it resolves itself. Part 3 borrows from Your Best Year Ever's "find your why." You don't need to have read either book.

Using an LLM here (encouraged, with one boundary)

Use an LLM to research and widen your options — summarize a real job posting, generate more mitigating strategies than you'd think of alone, or role-play what a day in that job might actually look like. Then decide for yourself and write the decision in your own words. An LLM writing the final answer for you defeats the point — grading rewards specific, personal reasoning over generic polish (see rubrics/A09_rubric.md).

What you will submit

A Canvas text entry (no file upload) with nine numbered answers, answered individually — don't merge them into one essay.

Part 1 — What you're eager for (the Desire Zone)

Q1. From your A05 dream job, what specific part of the work are you most eager for? Name the actual task or responsibility (not just "the job" or "the money"), and say why. (2 pts)

Q2. Which class, project, or experience — name it specifically — best prepares you for that part? (2 pts)

Q3. What's the best use of your time this semester to build toward it? (2 pts)

Part 2 — What will be hardest

Q4. What part of this career do you expect to be the most difficult? Name a specific skill, task type, or environment — not "it'll be hard." (2 pts)

Q5. List three mitigating strategies for that difficulty — a course, a habit, a person to ask, a project to attempt. Three genuinely different approaches, not one idea said three ways. (3 pts — 1 per distinct, real idea)

Q6. Which is your favorite — the one you'll actually act on? Why that one, and not the others? (2 pts)

Q7. Which class, skill, or experience between now and graduation most directly addresses this difficulty? (2 pts)

Q8. What's your concrete next step, and by when? (2 pts)

Part 3 — Why it matters

Q9. How does this career direction align with your values? Name one place of real fit, and one place of real tension — and how you'd resolve the tension. (3 pts)

Total: 20 points

Need help?

If you're between two target jobs, pick the one you named in A05 and answer for that one — you can revisit the other later.

See rubrics/A09_rubric.md for grading.
assignments.name: A09 — Career Reflection

rubric.long_description: Q1 (2 pts) — names a specific task/responsibility from the actual A05 job with a real personal reason, not "the job" or "the money." Q2 (2 pts) — a specific, real class/project/experience that prepares for it, not "my classes in general." Q3 (2 pts) — a concrete action this semester tied to that specific part of the job.

Q4 (2 pts) — names a specific difficult skill/task-type/environment, not "it'll be hard." Q5 (3 pts total, 1 pt per genuinely distinct mitigating strategy, up to 3 — three restatements of one strategy score 1, not 3) — three mitigating strategies. Q6 (2 pts) — a real reason for the favorite strategy, not "I don't know, this one."
Q7 (2 pts) — a specific, attainable-before-graduation class/skill/experience tied to the difficulty named in Q4. Q8 (2 pts) — a real next-step action with a real date, not "soon" or "eventually."
Names one specific point of fit and one specific point of tension, plus how the student would resolve it (one holistic 0–3 judgment, not sub-divided further).

assignments.description:
A07 — Advisor name and meeting time

Due: When registration/enrollment opens for next semester. (Exact date is set by the registrar's calendar each term — confirm the real date before publishing this to students.)

Why we're doing this

Your academic advisor is the person who can catch problems your degree plan (A03) and progress report (A02) can't — substitution rules, graduation-application deadlines, sequencing quirks specific to your program. Knowing who your advisor is and having an actual meeting on the calendar is a small task that prevents big problems later.

This is timed to when you can actually act on your advisor's guidance — right as registration for next semester opens, not buried earlier when there's nothing yet to register for.

What you will submit

A short Canvas text submission (no file upload required).

Requirements

  • Set up an appointment with your academic advisor.
  • Submit your advisor's name and the date of your upcoming meeting.
  • If you've had difficulties with your advisor in the past, briefly share what happened — that's useful, not a complaint that gets you in trouble.

If you don't know who your advisor is, or aren't happy with your current one

Reach out to your department chair. They can help you get connected to the right advisor — and it's fine to say plainly why you want a change.

Need help?

If anything about the appointment process is confusing or something unexpected comes up, message the instructor.

See rubrics/A07_rubric.md for grading.

assignments.description:
A10 (Optional / Bonus) — Success Foundations Reflection

This assignment is optional bonus work, not required. It has no fixed due date tied to A04–A06/A09 or the rest of Kickoff Week's Friday load — complete it whenever you like during the semester. (Earlier, this was briefly assigned as required, graded work due the same day as A04-A06/A09; Jeremy reversed that call the same day — see semester_kickoff_week/success_foundations_supplemental/README.md for the history.)

Why this is here

Building a resume (A04), naming a real target job (A05), and comparing your skills against it (A06) all raise the same question in the background: how do you actually get from where you are now to that job? This assignment lets you step back and think about that, using the mastery framework from the companion reading, success_foundations_reading.md (drawn from How Learning Works, Ch. 3). Complete the reading first; answer in your own words, not copied sentences from it.

What you will submit

A Canvas text entry (no file upload) with four numbered answers, 2–4 sentences each unless a question says otherwise.

Questions

  1. Recall/comprehension. The reading identifies three things learners need to develop mastery: component skills, integration/fluency of those skills, and knowing when/where to apply them. Pick one of the three and explain, in your own words, what it means and why it's not enough on its own. (3 pts)

  2. Recall/comprehension. What does the reading mean by "cognitive load," and what are the three types it names (intrinsic, extraneous, germane)? (2 pts)

  3. Application (required) — tie to A06. Use the same target job you named in A05/A06. Break the skill gap you identified in A06 into at least three component skills the way the reading describes breaking down "write a grant" or "analyze a case." Which of those component skills is currently your weakest, and how do you know? (3 pts)

  4. Application. The reading describes an "expert blind spot," where experienced people underestimate how much a novice needs explained. Describe one time you experienced this — either as the novice confused by an expert's shortcut, or as someone further along who caught yourself assuming something was obvious. (2 pts)

Total: 10 points (bonus)

These 10 points are real and gradable, but sit in Canvas's default, 0%-weighted assignment group rather than any of docs/grading-model.md's weighted categories — the same "ungrouped" placement A4 (Show and Tell reflection) uses. Whether points earned here can actually push a student's final percentage above 100% is a Canvas-mechanics question that depends on grading-scheme details this repo hasn't decided; treat this as "extra, optional, earns real points on record" rather than a confirmed boost to the final grade.

Source and Limitation Note

This assignment is derived from friday_entering_your_career/success_foundations_reading.md, itself drawn from How Learning Works, 2nd ed. (Ambrose, Bridges, DiPietro, Lovett, Norman), Chapter 3. No claims here go beyond what that reading already states.

See rubrics/A10_rubric.md for grading.

pages.title: Monday — Survive this semester
pages.body:
Monday — Survive this semester

Today's goal: launch day, not panic day.

Slides — Monday (PDF)

Good habits, not talent

What actually makes people successful in a demanding course isn't raw talent — it's a small set of habits:

  1. Small steps, tested often. Don't write (or plan, or build) a huge amount before checking your work. Check constantly.
  2. A clear debugging story: Expected → Actual → Tried. When something goes wrong — in code, in a proof, in a project, in life — you can name what you expected, what actually happened, and what you already tried. That's the difference between a bad help request and a good one: - Bad: "It doesn't work." - Good: "I expected X, I got Y, here's what I tried."
  3. Evidence over vibes. Screenshots, error messages, specific examples — not just a feeling that something is wrong.

If your own "debugging story" (about anything — tech or not) involved trying more than one thing before it worked, you're already doing this. That instinct is the whole skill; the rest is practice.

What this course actually is

(CS1 reference instance — replace per course, see docs/NAMING.md)

CS1 is problem solving, communication, and habits — not memorizing syntax. The building-block mindset: every program is made of small, testable pieces, assembled in order.

What's due this week

  • A01–A03 (unofficial transcript, progress report, degree plan) — due Wednesday
  • A04–A06 (resume, dream job paper, gap analysis) — due Friday by 4:00 PM

Split across the week on purpose, so it's not all due at once. Open the Week 1 Overview in Canvas and get familiar with what's expected.

Why Friday at 4:00 PM specifically: that's this term's last day to add a class without special permission. This whole week — transcript, degree plan, dream job, gap analysis — exists so you have real information about your major and your direction before that door closes, not after.

The full picture: 7 assignments, spread across the semester

A01–A06 aren't the whole story either — this course has 7 assignments total that build your degree and career readiness:

# Assignment Due
A01 Unofficial transcript This Wednesday
A02 Progress report This Wednesday
A03 Personal semester-by-semester degree plan This Wednesday
A04 Resume This Friday, 4:00 PM
A05 Dream Job Paper This Friday, 4:00 PM
A06 Professional Gap Analysis This Friday, 4:00 PM
A07 Advisor name and meeting time Later — when registration opens for next semester

You'll hear about A04–A07 again on Wednesday and Friday this week — this is just so nothing on that list is a surprise later.

Exit ticket

  1. One habit I'll practice, one reason it matters, and one action I'll take.
  2. Two things I'll do in the first 10 minutes when I get stuck.
  3. One question I have right now.

Go to the Monday Exit Ticket assignment — submit your answers there for real credit (10 points).

pages.title: Monday — Student activity: Debugging Story Drill
pages.body:
Monday — Student activity: Debugging Story Drill

In-class activity — no submission required. Do this live with a partner; nothing here is turned in on its own. The two habits you pick in Part 2 are what you'll write up for real credit on the Monday Exit Ticket right after this activity.

Part 1 — Tell your story (5 minutes)

Think of any time something didn't work — tech or non-tech, doesn't matter. Write 3 sentences:

  1. What I expected:
  2. What actually happened:
  3. What I tried:

Share with a partner, then be ready to share with the class.

Part 2 — Pick 2 habits and make them concrete (10 minutes)

From today's three "good habits" (small steps tested often; a clear debugging story; evidence over vibes), pick two and write:

Habit 1: ____

  • What it looks like when I do it well (give a real example):
  • What I'll do when I get stuck (name 3 steps):

Habit 2: ____

  • What it looks like when I do it well (give a real example):
  • What I'll do when I get stuck (name 3 steps):

Why this matters

A bad help request sounds like "it doesn't work." A good one sounds like "I expected X, I got Y, here's the error, here's the input, here's what I tried." If your Part 1 story already had you trying more than one thing, you already have the instinct — today is about making it deliberate.

pages.title: Wednesday — Thrive in your degree
pages.body:
Wednesday — Thrive in your degree

Today's goal: turn "I hope I graduate" into "I know my next steps."

Your unofficial transcript and progress report are the closest thing to "the truth in writing" about where you stand. They show what you've completed, what still remains, and where your gaps are. The same office that runs your graduation check produces both documents — knowing how to read them is a real, transferable skill, not a one-time chore.

What your transcript and progress report actually show

Your unofficial transcript is what you've done:

  • Courses taken, grades, credit hours
  • Transfer credit
  • Course completion history
  • Your GPA

Your progress report is what you still need — the registrar's own software reorganizes that same history against your specific degree requirements:

  • Areas/categories (Gen Ed, major core, electives, etc.)
  • What's satisfied vs. still outstanding in each area
  • Specific requirement blocks or substitutions still open

Why both matter here: prerequisites, sequencing, and your graduation timeline all depend on them together — the transcript shows where you've been, the progress report shows what's left. It's also a quick "how am I doing at this college thing?" check-in.

Degree plan = a map, not a prophecy

Plans change. The actual skill is updating the plan without panic when they do. Today you'll start a rough semester-by-semester grid: which courses, which semester, how many credits — and you'll get a classmate's eyes on it before you finalize anything.

Rules of thumb for building it:

  • Put required math/core courses early — prerequisites are gates, not suggestions.
  • Pick one hard class per semester, not four.
  • Balance heavy semesters — don't stack every difficult course together.
  • Summer classes are often online; some programs offer interim options too.
  • Leave breathing room. Life happens. Your plan should survive it.

A quick grounding technique, while we're at it

Box breathing: in 4 seconds, hold 4, out 4, repeat 4 times. When you're stressed, your brain lies to you about how much is actually wrong — this is how you take the wheel back before planning something as consequential as your degree path.

What's due today (by end of day)

  • A01 — Unofficial transcript (upload + short reflection)
  • A02 — Progress report (upload + short summary)
  • A03 — Personal semester-by-semester degree plan
  • A08 — Degree Reflection (nine short, individually-graded questions — what excites you, what worries you, and why it matters; see below)

Friday isn't a free pass — A04, A05, and A06 (resume, dream job paper, gap analysis) are due Friday by 4:00 PM. Today is just about getting the degree side finished and off your plate first.

About A08 — this isn't busywork

A01–A03 prove you can find and read your own data. A08 is where you actually think about what it means — separated out, on purpose, with its own points on each question, because a reflection buried at the end of another assignment is the easiest thing in this whole week to skip. It isn't optional. Nine short answers: three about the class you're most excited about, five working through the thing you're most afraid of (name it, brainstorm three ways to handle it, pick one, plan your time, tie it back to your career), and one about whether your degree plan actually reflects what you value. Full prompts in assignments/A08_degree_reflection.md.

Looking ahead: A07 — Advisor name and meeting time

Your advisor can catch things your transcript, progress report, and degree plan can't — substitutions, deadlines, sequencing quirks specific to your program. Nothing due yet — A07 lands later in the semester, timed to when registration for next semester actually opens, so the meeting happens right when you can act on the advice.

Exit ticket (answer in 2–4 sentences)

  1. One thing I learned about my transcript or degree progress, one concern, and one next step.
  2. Two courses I think I should take next (or two questions I have about sequencing).
  3. One thing I can do this week to reduce stress or stay on track.

pages.title: Wednesday — Student activity: Transcript Treasure Hunt + Degree Plan Start
pages.body:
Wednesday — Student activity: Transcript Treasure Hunt + Degree Plan Start

Part 1 — Transcript Treasure Hunt (5 minutes)

If you have transcript access today, use it. If not, answer from memory and mark uncertain items with a "?" — you'll confirm them for real in A01.

Step 1 — Find your total completed credit hours

Write down your total completed credit hours: ______

Step 2 — Self-check: which tier are you in?

This is a pass/fail self-check, not a test — there is exactly one tier below that's a genuine "flag it" answer. Every other tier is on-track or ahead of the curve.

Under 60 credit hours — building your foundation. You're early, and that's exactly where you should be. Worth knowing now: stacking an associate's degree along the way is a real, legitimate strategy — a lot of your core/gen-ed credit already counts toward one. It's not a fallback or a consolation prize; it's a credential-stacking move some students use deliberately, landing a real credential in hand before finishing the bachelor's. Ask your advisor whether your current course mix already lines up with one — if it does, claiming it costs you very little.

60 to 120 credit hours — you've got a lot of runway. You're in the normal middle of a multi-year plan. This is a good place to be. Keep using this week's habits — a real plan, prerequisites checked, one hard class per semester — to stay on track toward graduation.

Over 120 credit hours — flag this one for a real conversation. This is not "behind" or "failing" — there are plenty of good reasons a student lands here (a changed major, transfer credit that didn't map cleanly, a deliberately slower pace, a double major). But past roughly 120 hours you should either already be very close to done or have a specific, known reason why not. Put a real question about this in front of your advisor this semester — not because something is wrong, but because at this point a second set of eyes is worth having confirm your assumptions. A "wrong" answer here means exactly one thing: go have that conversation. It does not mean you're failing.

Which tier are you in? ______

A few more quick recall checks

  1. What math course are you in, or last completed?
  2. What courses in this subject area have you completed, if any?
  3. Any repeats or withdrawals that might matter?
  4. Using your progress report (not just the transcript): name one specific requirement area you still have outstanding.

Part 2 — Start your degree plan grid (10 minutes)

Build a rough grid: Semester → Courses.

Keep these rules of thumb in mind as you place courses:

  • Required math/core courses go early — prerequisites are gates.
  • Pick one hard class per semester, not four.
  • Balance heavy semesters against lighter ones.
  • Summer classes are often online.
  • Leave breathing room — your plan should survive real life happening.

Starting from a blank page? Use a scaffold.

Two generic starter grids are available if you'd rather fill in a structure than start from nothing:

Semester Course Type Course (fill in) Credit Hours Notes
Semester 1 (Fall) Math/Core Requirement Prerequisite gate — place early
Semester 1 (Fall) Major Requirement
Semester 1 (Fall) Gen Ed
Semester 1 (Fall) Elective
Semester 1 (Fall) Semester total Sanity-check against a manageable load
... Repeat this block per semester until graduation

Full 8-semester versions — one shaped generically around a CS-track's usual mix (math/core-heavy early, major requirements building through the middle), one shaped generically around an Engineering Technology track's usual mix (adds a Lab/Applied Requirement row type, reflecting that ET programs typically carry a heavier applied/lab credit load) — are in the course repo at semester_kickoff_week/templates/ (ask your instructor if you'd like the CSV to import into Google Sheets directly).

These are starting scaffolds, not an official degree audit. The category labels ("Major Requirement," "Gen Ed," etc.) are structural placeholders, not real course numbers — this repo does not have an authoritative, up-to-date copy of the actual degree catalog to pull real course numbers from. Fill in real course numbers from your institution's actual catalog/degree audit, and bring the result to your advisor to verify — the same "check with a real advisor" step Part 3 below and A03 both already ask for.

Part 3 — Partner check (5 minutes each way)

Swap grids with a partner and answer:

  1. What looks strong about this plan?
  2. What looks risky or confusing?
  3. One question you'd bring to an advisor about this plan.

This grid is prep for A03 — Personal semester-by-semester degree plan, due Friday — you're not finalizing anything today, just getting a real first draft and a second set of eyes on it.

pages.title: Friday — Entering your career
pages.body:
Friday — Entering your career

Today's goal: run your life like a project, and turn Week 1 into something submitted.

STAR bullets — achievement bullets, not duty bullets

You get to build your story on purpose: skills, projects, evidence. The shift is duties → achievements — not "what I was responsible for" but "what I accomplished, with evidence."

STAR in one breath:

  • Context (Situation/Task): the situation and task, in one short phrase.
  • Action: a strong verb — built, analyzed, designed, led.
  • Result: the "so what?" — ideally with a number.

Bullet formula: [Power verb] + [what you did / context] + [result or benefit].

Two examples:

  • "Resolved 15+ customer issues per shift, improving satisfaction and reducing manager escalations."
  • "Built a Python script to automate file cleanup, saving ~30 minutes per week."

SMART goals — a way to turn a wish into a plan

  • Specific — exactly what you'll do.
  • Measurable — how you'll track it.
  • Achievable — challenging but possible.
  • Relevant — matters to you right now.
  • Time-bound — a deadline.

"If you can't tell when you're done, it's not a goal yet."

Pomodoro — focus sprints

Your brain starts lying when a task feels big. Pomodoro makes the first step small: 15 minutes on, 5 minutes off (build up to 25/5 with experience). One task only. Phone away, notifications off. When distracted, write it down and come back to the work — don't chase it.

The 3-2-1 CV/resume habit — tiny, repeatable

  • 3 daily notes (wins, work, learning) — a running document you keep on your phone.
  • 2 weekly paragraphs in a running CV doc, written as STAR stories.
  • 1 monthly resume bullet — a measurable achievement.

Remember: CV = your full story. Resume = your best highlights for one job. Building the CV all semester means the resume is just curation later, not a panic-write the week before you need one.

What's due today, by 4:00 PM

  • A04 — Resume: a real, current resume, using STAR bullets, not duty bullets — the 3-2-1 habit above is what makes this easy instead of a scramble.
  • A05 — Dream Job Paper: name a specific, real job you could apply for, and why it's the one you want.
  • A06 — Professional Gap Analysis: compare your current skills against that job's real requirements, and build a plan to close the gap.
  • A09 — Career Reflection: nine short, individually-graded questions — what part of that job you're eager for, what part worries you, and why it matters (see below).

A01–A03 (transcript, progress report, degree plan) were due Wednesday — if you're missing one of those, get it in too, but today's focus is these three.

About A09 — this isn't busywork

Same idea as Wednesday's A08, career side: A04–A06 prove you can build a resume and compare yourself against a real job. A09 is where you think about what that job actually means for you — separated out, individually pointed, so it doesn't get skipped. Three questions about the part of the job you're genuinely looking forward to, five working through the hardest part (name it, find three ways to prepare, pick one, name your next step, tie it to a real class or skill), and one about whether this career direction actually fits your values. Full prompts in assignments/A09_career_reflection.md.

Getting started on A05 and A06

Both ask you to get specific, not hypothetical:

  • A05 (Dream Job Paper): don't pick "something in tech" — pick an actual job posting or job title you could apply for, now or later. A real posting (search any job board in your field) gives you real requirements to write about instead of guessing.
  • A06 (Gap Analysis): use the same job you picked for A05. List what you already have (hard and soft skills) next to what the job actually asks for, and be honest about the gap — that's the point of the assignment, not a flaw in it.

Full instructions are in each assignment file — this is just enough to get you started without overthinking the target.

4:00 PM matters: it's this term's last day to add a class without special permission. Everything this week — including today's three — exists so you have real information before that door closes, not after.

Looking ahead: A07 — Advisor name and meeting time

Not due today. A07 lands later in the semester, timed to when registration for next semester opens, so the meeting happens right when you can actually act on your advisor's advice.

Exit ticket

  1. What did you submit today (A01/A02/A03)?
  2. When is your next scheduled focus sprint for this class (day/time)?
  3. What's one thing you want help with next week?

pages.body:

pages.title: Building Real-World Mastery (optional supplemental reading)
pages.body:
Building Real-World Mastery (optional supplemental reading)

  • Essential question: How do successful professionals learn?
  • Status: optional supplemental material, not required reading. It lives in its own optional module rather than Kickoff Week's required Friday flow (STAR bullets, SMART goals, Pomodoro, the 3-2-1 CV habit, A04-A06/A09) — reversed out of that required flow 2026-08-08, the same day it was briefly placed there, because it made an already-dense Friday crushing. See semester_kickoff_week/success_foundations_supplemental/README.md for the full history.
  • Intended eventual form: Jeremy's plan is a short video/presentation companion to this reading (not yet recorded — this page is the reading alone until that exists).
  • Estimated reading time: approximately 7-9 minutes
  • Primary source: How Learning Works: Eight Research-Based Principles for Smart Teaching, 2nd edition, Ambrose, Bridges, DiPietro, Lovett, and Norman — Chapter 3, "How Do Students Develop Mastery?"
  • Perspective lens: none; single primary source, complete chapter.

Why This Matters Today

Everything else on today's agenda — the resume you're building, the dream job you're naming, the gap analysis comparing your skills to that job's real requirements — is really one question in disguise: how do you get good at something you're not good at yet? Professionals constantly have to develop new mastery: a new tool, a new role, a new domain, or a more complex version of work they already know. Unlike a structured course, professional life rarely provides a syllabus that identifies every component skill, explains how the pieces fit together, or specifies when a familiar approach will apply. Understanding how mastery actually develops helps you diagnose what you still need to learn, practice deliberately, and recognize when knowledge must be adapted to a new situation — which is exactly the gap your Gap Analysis (A06) asks you to name honestly.

What Mastery Requires

Primary-source claim: The chapter defines mastery as more than possessing individual facts or skills. To develop mastery, learners must acquire component skills, practice integrating them until they can be used fluently and with some automaticity, and know when and where to apply what they have learned (Chapter 3).

Responsible paraphrase: Complex professional tasks often contain hidden component skills. A task that appears to be "write a grant," "analyze a case," or "solve a problem" may require planning, recognizing relevant information, selecting an approach, executing procedures, and evaluating the result. If one of those component skills is weak or missing, performance on the larger task can suffer. Breaking a complex task into parts can reveal what needs targeted practice.

Primary-source claim: Practice with component skills may occur in isolation, within the whole task, or through a combination of both. For highly complex tasks whose parts can be meaningfully separated, isolated practice can help learners focus on a weak skill before progressively combining the parts. Whole-task practice is more useful when the task is relatively simple or when its components cannot realistically be separated. The learner's level of experience and the learning goal also matter (Chapter 3).

Responsible paraphrase: Knowing the parts is not enough. Learners must practice integrating them. Combining unfamiliar skills places demands on working memory, which the chapter describes as limited. Cognitive load increases when people must process many new elements at once. Experts often perform complex tasks more easily because extensive practice has made component skills more automatic; they do not necessarily have more cognitive capacity than novices.

Primary-source claim: Cognitive load includes the demands imposed by the task itself, distracting or poorly designed features unrelated to learning, and mental effort that supports deeper learning. The chapter identifies these as intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load. Clear directions, focused tasks, worked examples, scaffolding, temporary limits on complexity, and restrained use of new technologies can reduce unnecessary load while learners build fluency (Chapter 3).

Responsible paraphrase: Mastery also requires transfer: applying knowledge, skills, strategies, or habits learned in one context to a new context. Transfer does not happen automatically, especially when the original and new situations are dissimilar. Learners may depend on superficial cues from the original setting or memorize procedures without understanding the deeper principles that explain when those procedures apply.

Primary-source claim: Transfer is more likely when learners connect concrete experiences to abstract principles, apply skills across varied contexts, compare cases or problems to identify deep features, generate possible applications, and receive prompts that remind them of relevant prior knowledge. These practices help learners recognize when a familiar skill is appropriate in an unfamiliar situation (Chapter 3).

Responsible paraphrase: The chapter also identifies an "expert blind spot." Experts organize knowledge into large conceptual chunks, recognize patterns quickly, skip steps, and perform familiar tasks with little conscious effort. As a result, they may underestimate how long novices need to learn a task, omit steps that seem obvious, or assume that beginners can recognize the relevance of a skill across contexts. The same pattern can appear in professional life when someone who is highly experienced trains a new colleague — including, someday, you training someone newer than you.

A Concrete Example

Imagine a project coordinator learning to manage a client implementation at a software company — the kind of role you might name in today's Dream Job Paper (A05). At first, the coordinator must develop several component skills: learning the project-management platform, documenting requirements, tracking deadlines, communicating with the client, identifying risks, and escalating problems. Knowing each skill separately does not yet produce mastery. During a live implementation, the coordinator must integrate them while responding to changing priorities and unexpected technical issues.

The coordinator may also experience cognitive overload if the team introduces several unfamiliar tools, unclear procedures, and competing communication channels at the same time. Early practice with a simplified project and clear templates could reduce unnecessary demands while the coordinator builds fluency. Later, the coordinator must transfer the lessons from one client to another. A familiar process may not apply automatically if the second client has different constraints, stakeholders, or goals. Mastery therefore includes recognizing the underlying principles of good coordination and judging how they fit the new context. This is an invented illustration and my own synthesis of the chapter's framework, not an example attributed to the authors.

Synthesis

The chapter's central lesson is that successful learning is built deliberately. Professionals develop mastery by identifying the parts of complex work, strengthening weak component skills, practicing how those parts fit together, and learning to recognize the conditions in which their knowledge applies. The essential question is therefore not simply, "How much do I know?" It is also, "What can I do fluently, how do the parts work together, and how will I recognize when to use them?" That is the same lens today's SMART goals and Pomodoro focus sprints are meant to apply to your own semester, starting now.

Reflection Questions

  1. What professional skill are you currently developing, and what component skills make up that larger ability?

  2. Where might you be relying on knowledge from one context without yet knowing how to transfer it to another?

  3. Think of a task that currently feels cognitively overloaded. Which demands are essential to the learning or work, and which might be reduced, clarified, or practiced separately?

Source and Limitation Note

  • Primary source: Ambrose, Susan A., Michael W. Bridges, Michele DiPietro, Marsha C. Lovett, and Marie K. Norman. How Learning Works: Eight Research-Based Principles for Smart Teaching. 2nd edition. Chapter 3, "How Do Students Develop Mastery?"
  • This reading draws on one chapter as an "appetizer" selection, not the whole book.
